Criteria die na de demo worden opgesteld, beschrijven de demo.
Eigen scenario
Iedere leverancier hetzelfde scenario op jouw data, met dezelfde tijd.
Eigen referenties
Bel ook klanten die niet op de aangeleverde lijst staan.
remember: Je koopt geen functionaliteit, je koopt een relatie van drie jaar met een organisatie die verandert.
body:
Waarom AI-selectie anders is

Bij gewone software kun je functionaliteit afvinken. Bij AI-toepassingen is de kernvraag niet "kan het systeem dit?" maar "hoe goed doet het dit op mijn data, en wat gebeurt er als het ernaast zit?". Dat is een fundamenteel andere vraag, en de standaard-RFP is er niet op ingericht.

Daarbij komt dat demo’s in dit domein misleidend goed zijn. Een presentatie op zorgvuldig gekozen voorbeelden zegt weinig over prestaties op jouw rommelige werkelijkheid. Dit proces is ontworpen om dat verschil zichtbaar te maken.

Stap 1: Formuleer het besluit, niet de behoefte

Begin met de uitkomst die je wilt bereiken, uitgedrukt in je eigen proces. Niet "we zoeken een documentverwerkingsplatform" maar "we willen dat 80% van de binnenkomende dossiers binnen een dag compleet is, met minder handmatige controle dan nu".

Deze formulering houdt de deur open voor oplossingen die je nog niet kent, inclusief de mogelijkheid dat er geen aankoop nodig is.

Stap 2: Stel criteria en wegingen vast vóór de marktverkenning

Dit is de belangrijkste stap en degene die het vaakst wordt overgeslagen. Business, IT, security en inkoop bepalen samen welke criteria tellen en hoe zwaar, voordat er één leveranciersnaam op tafel komt.

Een werkbare set categorieën:

  • Functionele fit: dekt het jouw scenario’s af?
  • Prestatie op eigen data: hoe goed werkt het op jouw materiaal?
  • Integratie: hoeveel werk is koppelen met jouw systemen?
  • Data en privacy: waar staat de data, wat gebeurt ermee, wordt er op getraind?
  • Beheersbaarheid: kun je drempels, regels en uitzonderingen zelf aanpassen?
  • Kosten: licentie, verbruik, integratie, beheer, exit.
  • Leverancier: continuïteit, roadmap, ondersteuning in jouw taal en tijdzone.

Leg de wegingen schriftelijk vast en laat ze accorderen. Criteria die na de eerste demo worden bijgesteld, beschrijven die demo.

Stap 3: Maak een longlist op fit, niet op bekendheid

Zoek breder dan de drie namen die iedereen kent. Kijk naar gespecialiseerde partijen in jouw sector, naar wat er in je bestaande softwarelandschap al inzit (vaak meer dan je denkt), en naar de mogelijkheid om het met standaardcomponenten zelf samen te stellen.

Neem minimaal één "geen aankoop"-optie op in de vergelijking. Dat is geen formaliteit: het geeft je een referentiepunt voor wat de aankoop werkelijk toevoegt.

Stap 4: Stuur iedereen hetzelfde scenario

Geen open RFP met tweehonderd vragen. Stuur een concreet scenario: hier is een representatieve set van onze data (geanonimiseerd), dit is de taak, dit willen we terugzien. Dezelfde set, dezelfde vragen, dezelfde tijd voor iedereen.

De set moet representatief zijn, niet mooi. Neem de rommelige gevallen mee: onvolledige documenten, afwijkende formaten, randgevallen. Precies daar zit het verschil tussen leveranciers, en precies die gevallen ontbreken in elke demo.

Stap 5: Beoordeel onafhankelijk, bespreek daarna

Laat de beoordelaars hun scorecard individueel invullen voordat er gezamenlijk over wordt gesproken. Anders domineert de mening van de senior of de enthousiasteling, en verdwijnt de informatie uit de afwijkende oordelen.

Bespreek vooral de verschillen. Als twee beoordelaars hetzelfde antwoord heel anders scoren, betekent dat meestal dat het criterium niet scherp genoeg is. Dat wil je weten voordat je beslist.

Stap 6: Stel de vragen die het verschil maken

Een selectie van vragen die in de praktijk het meeste opleveren:

  • Wordt onze data gebruikt om jullie modellen te trainen? Zo ja, kunnen we dat uitzetten, en wat kost dat?
  • Welke onderliggende modellen gebruiken jullie, en wat gebeurt er als die leverancier zijn voorwaarden of prijzen wijzigt?
  • Hoe meten jullie kwaliteit, en mogen wij die meetmethode zien en reproduceren?
  • Wat gebeurt er als het systeem het fout heeft? Hoe merken wij dat, en wat is jullie aansprakelijkheid?
  • Kunnen wij zelf drempels en regels aanpassen, of moet dat via jullie?
  • Hoe krijgen wij onze data en configuratie eruit als we stoppen, in welk formaat en binnen welke termijn?
  • Welke klant die jullie vorig jaar verloren, mogen wij bellen?

Die laatste vraag levert zelden een naam op, maar de reactie erop zegt veel.

Stap 7: Reken de echte kosten uit

Een TCO over drie jaar, met minimaal deze posten: licentie, verbruikskosten bij verwacht én dubbel volume, eenmalige integratie, doorlopend beheer aan jouw kant, opleiding, en de geschatte exitkosten.

In de praktijk draait deze berekening de rangorde regelmatig om. De partij met het laagste licentietarief heeft vaak de duurste integratie, en verbruikskosten die bij volledige uitrol de licentie overstijgen.

Maak de berekening voor elke shortlistpartij op dezelfde manier en laat inkoop hem controleren. Een TCO die alleen de adviseur begrijpt, overleeft de eerste kritische vraag niet.

Stap 8: Onderhandel op wat je écht nodig hebt

De prijs is niet het belangrijkste onderhandelpunt. Belangrijker zijn:

  • Een prijsafspraak voor verbruik bij groei, zodat succes je niet onverwacht duur uitvalt.
  • Vastlegging van de exitvoorwaarden, inclusief formaat en doorlooptijd van dataoverdracht.
  • Een prestatieafspraak op jouw scenario, niet op een generieke SLA over beschikbaarheid.
  • Het recht om je eigen kwaliteitsmeting uit te voeren en de resultaten intern te gebruiken.
  • Duidelijkheid over wat er gebeurt als de leverancier het onderliggende model vervangt.

Dat laatste punt is nieuw ten opzichte van klassieke software en wordt bijna altijd vergeten. Leveranciers wisselen hun onderliggende modellen, soms zonder aankondiging, en dat kan de prestaties op jouw specifieke taak merkbaar veranderen, in beide richtingen. Leg vast dat je daarover wordt geïnformeerd en dat je dan opnieuw mag valideren.

Tot slot: documenteer waarom de anderen afvielen

Niet alleen waarom de winnaar won. De afvalredenen zijn het waardevolst als er over een jaar tegenvallers zijn en iemand vraagt waarom er niet voor partij B is gekozen. Zonder vastlegging wordt dat een gesprek over gevoel. Met vastlegging is het een gesprek over criteria die je destijds samen hebt bepaald.

title: Wanneer heb je echt een AI-strateeg nodig?
excerpt: In de helft van de gevallen is het antwoord: niet. Vier situaties waarin externe hulp loont, en vier waarin je het zelf beter kunt.
lede: Ik verdien mijn geld met AI-advies, dus lees dit met die wetenschap. Juist daarom staat er eerst in wanneer je me níét nodig hebt.
summary: Externe hulp loont bij onomkeerbare besluiten en interne patstellingen.
Bij afgebakende, technische vragen ben je intern vaak sneller.
Huur nooit iemand in om een besluit te legitimeren dat al genomen is.
summaryClose: De beste adviseur maakt zichzelf overbodig.
takeaways: Onomkeerbaarheid telt
Hoe moeilijker een besluit terug te draaien is, hoe meer een buitenstaander waard is.
Patstellingen doorbreken
Soms is de waarde niet de kennis, maar dat iemand zonder belang de knoop doorhakt.
Geen legitimatie kopen
Advies dat een besluit moet bevestigen, is weggegooid geld.
remember: Als je de vraag zelf scherp kunt stellen, kun je hem vaak ook zelf beantwoorden.
body:
Eerst: wanneer je het zelf beter kunt

Er zijn vier situaties waarin externe hulp weinig toevoegt, en waarin ik zelf doorverwijs of afhaak.

1. De vraag is technisch en afgebakend

"Welk model werkt het beste voor onze documentclassificatie?" is een vraag voor je eigen engineers of voor een gespecialiseerde bouwer. Een strateeg die daarop antwoord geeft, herhaalt wat je team al weet, tegen een hoger tarief.

2. Het besluit is klein en omkeerbaar

Een tool van honderd euro per maand voor één team, opzegbaar per maand? Probeer het gewoon. De tijd die je aan een afweging besteedt, kost meer dan het experiment. Bewaar analysekracht voor besluiten die je niet makkelijk terugdraait.

3. Je hebt al iemand die dit kan en het mandaat heeft

Als er een interne lead is met ervaring, budget en toegang tot de directie, dan is een externe adviseur meestal een extra laag in plaats van een versnelling. Geef die persoon ruimte in plaats van een sparringpartner die hij moet bijpraten.

4. Het besluit is al genomen

Dit is de vervelendste. Soms wordt advies ingekocht om een gekozen richting te bekrachtigen richting board of aandeelhouders. Dat is verspilling: voor de opdrachtgever, omdat er niets nieuws uit komt, en voor de adviseur, omdat elke afwijkende bevinding wordt weggemasseerd. Als ik dit patroon herken, benoem ik het. Soms blijkt er dan alsnog een echte vraag onder te zitten.

Wanneer externe hulp wél loont

1. Het besluit is duur en moeilijk terug te draaien

Een meerjarig platformcontract, een architectuurkeuze waar tien toepassingen op gaan leunen, een make-or-buy-beslissing voor iets wat je kernproces raakt. De kosten van een verkeerde keuze zijn hier een veelvoud van de adviesinvestering.

Een vuistregel: als de verkeerde keuze je meer dan tien keer het adviesbudget kost, en je bent er niet zeker van, dan is een second opinion een rationele verzekering.

2. Er is een interne patstelling

Twee afdelingen met een verschillende voorkeur, beide met goede argumenten, al maanden. Hier is de waarde van een buitenstaander niet primair zijn kennis, maar zijn afwezigheid van belang. Iemand die volgende maand weer weg is, kan een conclusie trekken die intern politiek beladen zou zijn.

Dit werkt alleen als de opdracht en de criteria vooraf door beide partijen zijn geaccepteerd. Anders verplaats je het conflict naar de kwaliteit van het advies.

3. Je moet iets aan een board of toezichthouder uitleggen

Als je een investering moet verdedigen bij mensen die er niet dagelijks mee bezig zijn, helpt een onafhankelijke onderbouwing. Niet omdat jouw analyse slechter is, maar omdat een externe toets de discussie verplaatst van "geloven we deze persoon" naar "klopt deze redenering".

Let op dat dit iets anders is dan legitimatie kopen. Het verschil: hier staat de uitkomst nog open.

4. Je hebt dit nog nooit gedaan en de tijdsdruk is hoog

De eerste keer dat een organisatie een AI-selectie doet, een AI-governancestructuur opzet of een AI-portfolio prioriteert, kost het twee tot drie keer zoveel tijd als de tweede keer. Iemand die het vaker heeft gedaan, koopt je die leercurve af. Dat is een legitieme reden, mits je de kennis daarna zelf houdt.

Wat je moet vragen voordat je iemand inhuurt

  • Wat is de kleinste opdracht waarmee we kunnen beginnen? Een goede adviseur biedt een instap van beperkte omvang aan. Wie meteen een traject van zes maanden voorstelt, verkoopt capaciteit.
  • Wanneer ben je klaar? Er hoort een antwoord te zijn dat niet "dat hangt ervan af" luidt.
  • Wat houden wij over als je weg bent? Documenten zijn het minimum. Kaders die je zelf kunt hergebruiken, zijn beter.
  • Welk deel van deze opdracht kunnen we zelf doen? Het antwoord hierop zegt meer over iemands integriteit dan elke referentie.
  • Welke belangen heb je? Partnerschappen, commissies, implementatiepraktijk. Vraag het expliciet en vraag om het op papier.

De omvang die meestal klopt

Voor de meeste organisaties geldt: een afgebakende opdracht van twee tot zes weken, of een deeltijdrol van een paar dagen per maand. Trajecten die langer duren zonder tussentijdse beslismomenten, zijn zelden in het belang van de opdrachtgever.

En als je twijfelt of je het nodig hebt: probeer de vraag eerst zelf op één pagina te formuleren, met de opties en de criteria. Lukt dat, dan is de kans groot dat je hem zelf kunt beantwoorden. Lukt het niet, dan weet je precies waar een gesprek over zou moeten gaan. En dat is een goed begin, of je nu iemand inhuurt of niet.

title: AI agents: what they can and cannot do in a business process
excerpt: Agents that carry out tasks independently are the promise of the moment. Where they work, where they break down, and the question you need to answer first.
metaTitle: What AI Agents Can and Cannot Do
metaDescription: Where AI agents work well, where they break down, and the one question you need to answer before handing a business process over to one.
lede: An agent that takes its own steps and calls on systems is attractive and risky at the same time. The distinction lies in what happens when it gets it wrong.
summary: Agents work well on reversible steps with a clear final check.
They break down on processes where a mistake propagates silently.
Start with preparing and proposing, not with executing.
summaryClose: Decide what a mistake costs first, then how much autonomy you give.
takeaways: Reversibility as the test
Give autonomy on steps you can undo without damage.
An agent is a process, not a tool
The question isn't which model, but which steps you hand over.
Logging is not optional
Without a full record of the steps taken, you cannot reconstruct a mistake.
remember: Autonomy isn't a property of the model, it's a choice the organisation makes.
body:
What makes an agent different

A standard AI application receives an instruction and gives an answer. An agent receives a goal and decides for itself which steps are needed: retrieving information, consulting a system, assessing an intermediate result, choosing a next step. That makes it more powerful, and it changes the risk question fundamentally.

With a standard answer, you assess one outcome. With an agent, you assess a chain in which a mistake in step two carries through to step five, possibly without the final output looking wrong. That is exactly where things go wrong in practice.

Where agents work well

Preparatory work with a clear final check

Gathering and organising information that a person then makes a decision on. Putting together a file from five sources, building a market overview, preparing a tender response. The agent does the search work, the person does the assessment.

This works because the mistake is visible at the moment it matters: the reviewer sees that something is missing or wrong, before anything irreversible happens.

Steps you can undo without damage

Drafting a concept, assigning a category that can be changed later, creating an internal note. If it goes wrong, you correct it and lose, at most, some time.

Routes with a hard, checkable outcome

If an objective test exists (a calculation that is right or wrong, a query that returns results or doesn't, a file that validates or doesn't), an agent can iterate independently until that test passes. The test is the safety valve.

Where agents break down

Processes where a mistake propagates silently

This is the most important category to avoid. If a wrong intermediate step leads to a final result that looks plausible, nobody discovers the mistake: not in the review, and not in the reporting. Financial processing, risk assessment, and anything where a number flows through to another system falls into this category.

Actions with external consequences

Sending a message to a customer, placing an order, changing an appointment, initiating a payment. Not because an agent can't technically do this, but because the cost of a mistake lands outside your organisation and you cannot take it back. A confirmation step belongs here as standard.

Long chains without an intermediate check

The more steps without a checkpoint, the greater the chance that the agent makes a wrong assumption somewhere halfway through and keeps building on it consistently. Practical limit: if there are more than a handful of steps without any check, build in an intermediate review, automated or human.

Situations without a complete log

If you cannot reconstruct which steps the agent took, which sources it consulted and why it chose a particular route, you cannot investigate an incident. For regulated processes that is not an option, and for everything else it's unwise.

The autonomy level as a deliberate choice

Autonomy is not a property of the technology but a setting you choose. Four levels, in ascending order:

  • Preparing: the agent gathers and organises, a person does everything after that. Lowest risk, often already the biggest time saving.
  • Proposing: the agent makes a concrete proposal including reasoning, a person approves or amends it.
  • Executing with confirmation: the agent takes the steps but asks for confirmation at the irreversible moments.
  • Acting independently: the full chain without intervention, with monitoring afterwards. Only for reversible steps with a hard final check.

My advice is almost always to start at level one or two, even if the model can handle more. Not out of caution, but because that's the phase in which you learn which mistakes actually occur. You need that knowledge to decide where you can safely increase autonomy, and you won't get that information anywhere else.

The question you need to answer first

For every step you hand over to an agent, one question: if this step goes wrong, who notices, when, and what does it cost to fix?

Three possible answers and what they mean:

  • Immediately visible, cheap to fix: give autonomy.
  • Visible later, fixable: autonomy with monitoring and a periodic sample check.
  • Not visible, or not fixable: no autonomy, full stop.

What this means in practice

The applications I see working in production are rarely the spectacular ones. They are agents that prepare files, bring together information from different systems, or draft a first version that a person finishes. The time saving is real (often tens of per cent on the preparatory step), and the risk is manageable because someone always looks at it before it matters.

The applications that fail are the chains that were given too much independence too soon. Not because the technology couldn't handle it, but because nobody had established what would happen if it got something wrong. That question takes half an hour, and determines whether your application is still running a year from now.

title: From AI strategy to value: a 3-step plan
excerpt: Most AI strategies don't fail on the strategy itself, but on translating it. Three steps that force that translation.
metaTitle: From AI Strategy to Value: A 3-Step Plan
metaDescription: Why most AI strategies stall after the document is written, and the three translation steps that turn direction into measurable results.
lede: A strategy nobody can execute is an expensive document. These are the three steps that turn direction into results, with the pitfall at each step.
summary: Translate ambition into measurable business outcomes, not technology.
Give each use case one owner with budget and a mandate.
Measure value at the same level you promised it.
summaryClose: Without an owner and a measurement point, every strategy stays an intention.
takeaways: Start with the outcome
"We're cutting handling time by 30% without satisfaction dropping" beats "we're applying AI to customer contact."
One owner per use case
Shared ownership is, in practice, no ownership at all.
Measure what you promised
If the business case was about pounds, user numbers aren't proof.
remember: A strategy only becomes real the moment someone turns it into a quarterly target.
body:
Where it goes wrong between strategy and results

I rarely see a bad AI strategy. What I do often see: a perfectly good strategy that, nine months later, is still exactly the same document, with the same ambitions and not a single result delivered. Not through unwillingness, but because three translation steps are missing that nobody has explicitly assigned.

Those three translation steps aren't a methodology. They're three questions you need to be able to answer before a strategy becomes executable.

Step 1: Translate ambition into business outcomes

Most AI strategies are written in technology language: "we're deploying generative AI for customer contact", "we're building a data-driven decision culture". Those are directions, not outcomes. You can't turn them into a quarterly target, and you can't steer by them.

The translation that works looks like this:

  • From: "using AI for customer contact", to: "average handling time for first-line queries down from 8 to 5 minutes, with customer satisfaction unchanged."
  • From: "predictive maintenance", to: "unplanned downtime on lines 3 and 4 down 20% within twelve months."
  • From: "increasing knowledge-worker productivity", to: "two hours per consultant per week freed up, redeployed to billable work."

The difference looks cosmetic. It isn't. The right-hand column forces you to decide who's accountable, what data you need to measure it, and when you'll conclude it isn't working. The left-hand column leaves all those questions open, and that is exactly why those strategies stall.

The pitfall here: formulating outcomes so ambitious that nobody dares to claim them. A goal nobody wants to attach their name to isn't a goal.

Step 2: Assign ownership with budget and a mandate

This is the step that gets skipped most often, usually with the best intentions. The use case gets "assigned to a working group" or "picked up jointly by IT and the business". In practice, that means: when it gets difficult, everyone looks at each other.

Ownership that works has three characteristics:

  • One name. Not a department, not a duo. One person who explains in the steering group why it is, or isn't, moving forward.
  • Budget in their own line. If the owner has to go through someone else for every pound, that someone else is the real owner.
  • A mandate to stop. This is almost always forgotten. An owner who is only allowed to continue is an executor.

A practical test: can you name the owner of every use case on your roadmap within ten seconds? If not, that use case doesn't have one.

The pitfall here: placing ownership with the AI lead or the data team. They can build and advise, but they aren't the ones sitting on the P&L where the value has to land. The owner belongs in the business, even when that's uncomfortable because that person has no AI background.

Step 3: Measure at the level you promised

This is where most of the quiet disappointment happens. The business case promised £400,000 in savings. The reporting shows: 1,200 active users, 87% satisfaction, 40,000 documents processed. All true, all positive, and none of it an answer to the question that was asked.

Usage statistics are useful as an early indicator. They are not proof of value. If your business case was formulated in pounds or hours, you ultimately need to report in pounds or hours too, even when that's harder to measure.

Three measurement layers that work together:

  • Adoption (weekly active users, usage per scenario): tells you whether people are using it.
  • Process performance (lead time, error rate, rework): tells you whether it's working.
  • Business outcome (cost, revenue, capacity): tells you whether it delivered anything.

The third layer almost always requires a baseline measurement you should have taken before you started. Take that baseline measurement. It's two days' work, and without those two days you can't prove anything a year later.

The pitfall here: only measuring what happened to already be on a dashboard. That's how you end up with a report full of usage figures.

What this delivers in practice

These three steps aren't complicated. They're uncomfortable. They force you to shrink ambitions down to something someone is willing to put their name to, and to establish in advance when you would conclude that it hasn't worked.

That's exactly why they work. A portfolio of four use cases with owners, measurement points and stop criteria delivers more than a roadmap with twenty initiatives everyone is enthusiastic about and nobody is accountable for.

title: Build, buy or partner: what fits your situation?
excerpt: The question is rarely "can we build this ourselves?" but "do we still want to be maintaining this in three years?" A decision framework in four questions.
metaTitle: Build, Buy or Partner for AI: A Decision Framework
metaDescription: A four-question framework for choosing between building AI yourself, buying it, or partnering, with the maintenance costs most people skip.
lede: Build it yourself, buy it, or partner with someone? The choice determines your cost structure, your agility and your dependency for years. Here's how to make it an informed one.
summary: Only build what sets you apart in the market.
Buy everything that's a commodity, even if you can build it yourself.
Partner where you want to steer the outcome but don't want to own the technology.
summaryClose: The maintenance question matters more than the build question.
takeaways: Distinctive or not?
If your competitor can buy it tomorrow, don't build it yourself.
Calculate to year five
Building is cheap in year one and expensive from year three.
Design the exit in
For every choice: how do you get out of it, and what does that cost?
remember: You're not building software, you're adopting a maintenance obligation.
body:
Why this choice weighs heavier with AI

With classic software, build-or-buy was mainly a cost question. With AI, three extra factors make the trade-off structurally different.

First, the underlying technology changes faster than your depreciation period. A model you fine-tune yourself today can be overtaken within eighteen months by a generic model that does it better out of the box, and more cheaply. Second, maintenance is fundamentally different: models quietly degrade as reality shifts, which calls for permanent monitoring rather than occasional patching. Third, the value often doesn't sit in the model but in your data and your working process, and you can't buy either of those anyway.

The four questions that decide the choice

Question 1: Is this distinctive, or is it a commodity?

The only good reason to build it yourself is that it sets you apart in the market. Not that it's fun, not that your team can do it, and not that it looks cheaper.

A hard test: can your main competitor buy the same result from a supplier tomorrow? If the answer is yes, it's a commodity, however technically interesting it is. Document extraction, speech recognition, summarising, standard classification: all commodities. The way you combine those building blocks with your own data and processes: that's where the distinction can lie.

In practice, at most ten to twenty per cent of what organisations want to build is genuinely distinctive. The rest gets built because it can be.

Question 2: What does it cost in year five?

Building is cheap in year one. You have a team, it builds something, it works. The costs that come after are rarely counted in:

  • Model monitoring and retraining as the data shifts
  • Keeping up with the underlying models and API versions
  • Security, logging and audit trail
  • Documentation and knowledge transfer when people leave
  • The opportunity cost of engineers maintaining this instead of building something new

A rule of thumb from practice: the annual maintenance of a self-built AI application runs between 20% and 40% of the original build cost. Run that through for five years and compare it to a licence. The conclusion often reverses.

Question 3: Who needs to be able to steer the outcome?

This is the question that justifies partnering. There are applications where you don't need to own the technology, but you do need influence over how the outcome comes about. Think of risk models, pricing, or anything that communicates towards customers on behalf of your brand.

A standard product rarely gives you that influence. Building it yourself gives you full influence but also the full burden. A partnership arrangement (where a supplier builds and manages, but you set the rules, thresholds and evaluation criteria) sits in between. It works if you arrange it well contractually, and it goes wrong if you run it on trust.

Question 4: How do you get out of it again?

The exit question belongs in the design, not in the renewal discussion three years from now. For each of the three options, exit looks different:

  • Build: exit means finding someone who understands your codebase. The risk sits in key-person dependency and missing documentation.
  • Buy: exit means getting your data and your configured logic out. Establish the format and the timeframe before signing.
  • Partner: exit means handover of both the build and the knowledge. Include a handover clause with a concrete deliverable, not an intention.

The hybrid form that works most often

In most projects I guide, the answer isn't one of the three in pure form. The setup that holds up most often:

  • Buy the building blocks. Models, infrastructure, standard components. This is where suppliers have economies of scale you'll never match.
  • Build the layer that holds your knowledge. The rules, the prompts, the evaluation sets, the link to your processes. This is small in scope and large in value.
  • Partner for implementation. But keep ownership of the evaluation criteria yourself.

Concretely: an organisation automating document processing buys the language model and the platform, builds its own field-extraction rules and a test set of two hundred assessed files, and has the integration done by a partner. The test set is the most valuable part and costs the least money.

Three situations where the choice is clear

Build if it touches directly on why customers choose you, you have exclusive access to the data, and you have a team that can still maintain this in five years.

Buy if there are three or more serious suppliers, the functionality is stable, and your main concern is time to value.

Partner if the technology is mature but the application is sensitive, and you want to steer the outcome but not the codebase.

Still unsure? Then buying is almost always the cheapest way to learn what you actually need. You can still build later, with a sharper specification and without losing a year.

title: Which AI use cases actually deliver results?
excerpt: Not the most spectacular, but the most boring. Four traits the winners share, and four patterns that almost always stall.
metaTitle: Which AI Use Cases Actually Deliver Results?
metaDescription: Four traits that separate AI use cases that deliver results from the ones that stall, drawn from dozens of use-case inventories.
lede: After dozens of use-case inventories, the same pattern stands out: the winners are rarely the ideas the board gets excited about. Here's what they do have in common.
summary: High volume, low variation, clear cost of error.
A human check already in the process, cheaper than the mistake.
Data that already exists and is already in use.
summaryClose: Boring and frequent beats spectacular and rare.
takeaways: Volume over complexity
Ten thousand small time savings beat one big insight.
The mistake has to be affordable
If a mistake is unrecoverable, the business case is much smaller than it looks.
Existing data wins
Every use case that requires new data collection pushes a year back.
remember: The best use case is usually the one nobody wants to give a presentation about.
body:
The pattern behind the winners

In use-case sessions, the same kind of ideas always float to the top: a chatbot that knows everything, a system that predicts the market, an assistant that makes meetings unnecessary. They're appealing because they sound big. They stall because they're vague.

The use cases that do make it share four traits. None of those traits is about technology.

1. High volume, low variation

A task that occurs a thousand times a month in roughly the same way is a better candidate than a task that occurs ten times a year and is different every time, even if that second task is more expensive per occurrence.

The reason is practical: at high volume, a small improvement pays for itself quickly, you can measure quickly whether it works, and there's enough material to improve the system. At low frequency, it takes a year before you know whether you have anything.

A concrete example: summarising customer calls (thousands a month, similar structure) is a better first use case than drafting the annual plan, however valuable that annual plan is.

2. The cost of a mistake is known and affordable

Every AI application makes mistakes. The question isn't whether, but what that mistake costs and who notices it. This question gets skipped too often, and it determines after the fact whether the use case is sustainable.

Three categories:

  • Affordable and visible: a wrongly suggested summary that the user sees and corrects immediately. Ideal candidate.
  • Affordable but invisible: a slightly wrong stock forecast that only shows up in the quarterly figures. Usable, provided you set up monitoring.
  • Costly and invisible: a wrongly rejected credit application. Only do this with a solid control structure, and rarely as a first use case.

3. There's already a human check in the process

This may be the strongest predictive trait. If someone in the current process already reviews, checks or signs off, you already have the most important safeguard in place. You're changing that person's role from doer to checker, and that's a much smaller change than it sounds.

Conversely: if a process runs fully automatically with no human involvement, and you want to put AI into it, you'll need to add that check yourself. That costs time, money and buy-in, and it makes the business case smaller than the original calculation suggested.

4. The data already exists and is already in use

Not "the data is available", but "the data is already used to make decisions". That difference is significant. Data already in use has already been cleaned up, already defined, and already has an owner. Data that sits somewhere but isn't used for anything is almost always worse quality than everyone assumes.

A use case that starts with "first we need to collect data" pushes back at least a year. Sometimes that's the right investment, but then call it a data project, not an AI use case.

Four patterns that almost always stall

The assistant that can do everything

"We're giving everyone an AI assistant" isn't a use case, it's a licence. Without defined scenarios, usage stays stuck around ten per cent, and then the organisation concludes that AI "doesn't work". Pick three to five concrete tasks, build ready-made starting points for them, and only add freedom later.

The prediction model with no decision behind it

A prediction nobody acts on is an expensive dashboard. Before you start: who looks at this prediction, what does that person do differently at outcome A versus outcome B, and do they have the mandate to do it? If any one of those three answers is missing, stop.

The use case with no owner in the business

If the only enthusiast sits in the innovation team or the data team, and there's nobody in the business who benefits, the use case won't survive the first reorganisation. Find the person whose quarterly target becomes more achievable because of it. If you can't find them, it's a nice idea, not a priority.

The use case that automates a process you should scrap instead

This is the most painful one. On analysis, it regularly turns out that the process we want to speed up mainly exists because another system is poorly set up. AI then makes that process cheaper, which means nobody ever scraps it. Always ask first: why does this step exist, and what happens if it disappears?

A practical scoring question

When prioritising a list, there are usually five questions I score each use case against, from 1 to 5:

  • How often does this task occur? (volume)
  • How predictable is the shape of the task? (variation)
  • Does the data needed already exist, and is it in use? (data readiness)
  • Is there already a check in place, or do we need to add one? (safety)
  • Is there an owner in the business who benefits? (pull)

Use cases that score below 15 points don't go first. Not because they're bad, but because your first two use cases need to succeed: the rest of your roadmap depends on it.

title: Independent AI consultant vs agency vs Big 4
excerpt: A fair comparison on independence, speed, depth, cost and delivery power, so you choose the right partner, even when that isn't me.
metaTitle: Independent AI Consultant vs Agency vs Big 4
metaDescription: An honest, practical comparison of independent AI consultants, agencies and Big Four firms on speed, cost, depth and delivery, so you choose the right partner.
lede: Which option fits your AI question best? A comparison on seniority, flexibility, focus, cost and delivery power.
summary: Independent consultant = senior, flexible and ready to start immediately.
Agency = specialist depth and delivery capacity.
Big 4 = governance, assurance and international coverage.
summaryClose: Choose based on your goal, time pressure and capacity for change.
takeaways: Seniority makes the difference
With an independent consultant, you always work with the senior person you spoke to. With larger firms, that's never guaranteed.
Speed and flexibility
A one-person practice can adjust scope within a week. A framework contract can't.
Pay for impact, not overhead
Fewer layers doesn't automatically mean better, but it does mean you know where your money goes.
remember: The best choice isn't the biggest firm, but the one that best fits your question, context and pace.
body:
When do you choose which?

AI projects differ sharply in purpose, complexity and context. The choice between an independent consultant, an agency or a Big 4 firm has a direct impact on speed, agility, cost and outcome. No single option wins on every measure, and anyone who claims otherwise is selling you something.

I'm the independent consultant in this line-up myself. That doesn't make me objective, so read this piece with that in mind. What I can do is be honest about the cases where you're better off not calling me. They're all in here.

1. The differences at a glance

CriteriaIndependent AI consultantAgencyBig 4
SeniorityAlways seniorVariesVaries
FlexibilityVery highAverageLow
Lead timeFastAverageLong
Cost structureTransparent & leanDepends on projectHigh (overhead)
ScalabilityLimitedHighVery high
FocusImpact & outcomeSolution & deliveryGovernance & assurance
Best suited forFocused AI initiativesBespoke work & specialismsTransformation & compliance

2. What does this mean in practice?

Independent AI consultant

You work directly with a senior expert who adapts quickly and does only what's genuinely needed. You get one opinion, not a negotiated position.

Agency

You bring in specialist capacity and build methodically. Ideal for bespoke work and scalable delivery, especially if you don't have your own engineering team.

Big 4

You choose assurance, governance and worldwide coverage. Suited to large transformations, mergers and projects where compliance leads.

Where the independent consultant wins

On focused, decision-driven questions. A strategy sprint, a vendor selection, a second opinion on a business case, a fractional leadership role. Work where one experienced head is worth more than ten pairs of hands. The lead time is shorter because there's no internal alignment needed between consultants, and the senior you spoke to at the introductory call is the same person who does the work.

Where the independent consultant loses

As soon as volume is needed. An implementation with eight developers, a migration across fifteen countries, a programme that runs for two years: I can't deliver that, and shouldn't try to. On projects sensitive to a single point of failure, a one-person practice is also a real risk: if I'm out for three months, you have a problem. An agency or Big 4 firm doesn't have that problem.

Where agencies are underestimated

Agencies sometimes get accused of mainly wanting to build. That's fair: it's their business model. But if you already know what you want to build, that's exactly what you need. A good agency brings engineering discipline, reusable components, and a team that has taken this type of system into production more than once. Don't underestimate how much that's worth.

Where the Big 4 are underestimated

The criticism of large consultancies is well known: expensive, lots of junior staff, thick reports. That happens. But on projects where the board carries liability, where regulators are watching, or where a decision has to clear an audit committee, you're buying something an independent consultant can't deliver: institutional cover and a methodology that's audit-proof. That's not overhead, that's the product.

Start small, learn fast and scale with focus. That's how you make AI workable and valuable.

3. The conflict-of-interest conversation

With AI, this goes further than with ordinary advisory work, because many advisers are also implementation partners for specific platforms. That isn't automatically wrong. A firm that builds a platform every day knows more about it than someone assessing it from a distance. But you need to know whether that's the case.

Ask every party these four questions, regardless of size:

  • Do you receive any fee, discount or partner status from suppliers who might be recommended in this project?
  • Do you have an implementation practice on the platforms that could end up on the shortlist?
  • What's your revenue split between implementation and advisory work?
  • Is the consultant who writes the advice rewarded on follow-on revenue?

Honest answers to these questions matter more than the answer itself. A firm that says "we're an implementation partner for three platforms, and here's how we account for that" is more trustworthy than one that claims to be "fully independent" without backing it up.

4. How do you make the right choice?

Answer these questions and you'll know faster which option fits best:

  • What's the primary goal: making a decision, building something, or demonstrably being in control of something?
  • How urgent is the lead time, and what does delay cost?
  • What level of governance and compliance is required, and who's watching?
  • Do you have in-house capability to build alongside and maintain it afterwards?
  • What's the available budget, and how much flexibility do you need in it?
  • What happens if the chosen party drops out halfway through?

5. The combination that often works best

In practice, I rarely see a clean choice. The setup that works out best most often: an independent senior handles the strategy and the selection, and an agency or systems integrator does the build, with the adviser on the client's side of the table during the build. The adviser then has no stake in the implementation's scope growing, which removes exactly the tension that otherwise shows up around month four.

It costs you a bit more in advisory hours. It usually saves you a multiple of that in extra work.

title: The role of the data foundation in successful AI initiatives
excerpt: "Get your data in order first" is as often an excuse as it is a necessity. How to work out which one applies to you.
metaTitle: The Data Foundation Under Successful AI Initiatives
metaDescription: "Get your data in order first" is as often an excuse as a necessity. How to work out which applies to your AI initiative, and what to do about it.
lede: The most common advice in AI is also the most dangerous: get your data in order first. Sometimes that's right. Often it's a way to do nothing for another two years.
summary: You don't need a perfect data foundation, you need enough foundation for one use case.
Definitions matter more than volume or infrastructure.
Build the foundation alongside a use case, not ahead of it.
summaryClose: Getting data in order with no application attached is a project with no end.
takeaways: Foundation per use case
Don't ask "is our data in order?" Ask "is this data good enough for this decision?"
Definitions first
Four systems with three definitions of "customer" is a bigger problem than a missing data warehouse.
Lineage counts
With AI, you need to be able to explain where a number came from. That's a governance question, not a technical one.
remember: A data foundation that isn't pulled forward by a concrete application never gets finished.
body:
Two truths that contradict each other

The first: without reliable data, AI delivers unreliable outcomes. That's not in dispute.

The second: organisations that want their entire data landscape in order before they start with AI rarely get to AI at all. The data foundation is never finished, after all, and there's always another layer that should come first.

Both are true. The way out is in how you phrase the question. "Is our data in order?" is a question you can't answer. "Is this data good enough to base this specific decision on?" you can answer, within a week.

What actually matters

When I run data scans ahead of AI projects, I come across four problems. They're not equally serious and they don't need the same fix.

Problem 1: Definitions (serious, often underestimated)

Four systems, three definitions of "customer". Two departments that calculate "revenue" differently. A product code that's a variant in one system and a separate product in another. This is by far the most common problem, and the most underestimated.

It's serious because no amount of technology fixes it. A model trained on inconsistently defined data learns that inconsistency too. And it's underestimated because everyone works consistently within their own department. The problem is only visible once you look across departments.

Approach: define only the five to ten terms that your use case touches. Not the whole company data model. That's two weeks of work instead of two years.

Problem 2: Lineage and traceability (serious for regulated work)

Can you trace a number in a report back to where it came from and what's been done to it? For AI applications that influence decisions, this isn't a luxury. Regulators, auditors and eventually your own board will ask that question.

Approach: map the lineage for the data flows your use case actually uses. Document the transformations. That doesn't need an expensive tool: a readable document that's accurate is worth more than a lineage tool nobody maintains.

Problem 3: Quality and completeness (manageable)

Missing fields, inconsistent entry, historical data that changed format halfway through. Annoying, but this is the type of problem technology actually helps with, and one you can quantify.

Approach: measure it. What percentage of records has the field you need? If it's 94%, you can get moving, and the question becomes what to do with the remaining 6%. If it's 40%, you're having a different conversation.

Problem 4: Accessibility and infrastructure (usually the least urgent)

No central data warehouse, data spread across systems, no APIs. This feels like the biggest problem because it's the most visible, and because suppliers are happy to sell you a platform for it. In practice, it's often the easiest to solve, especially for one use case.

Approach: for a first use case, a daily export is often enough. Don't build a platform to test a hypothesis.

The use-case-led order

The approach that works in practice reverses the order. You don't build the foundation upfront, you pull it along with your first applications.

  • Step 1: Choose one use case with clear value and an owner in the business.
  • Step 2: Map which data that use case actually needs: usually three to seven sources, not thirty.
  • Step 3: Fix the definitions, lineage and quality for those sources only. Do this properly, because it becomes your reference.
  • Step 4: Build the use case and measure whether it works.
  • Step 5: Choose the next use case that reuses as many of the same sources as possible.

After three or four use cases, you have a foundation that's grown out of real use. It's smaller than the ideal picture, and considerably more reliable, because every component is tested in production.

When "data first" is the right answer

There are situations where delaying really is wise. Three signals:

  • The core entity isn't clearly defined. If you can't pin down who counts as a customer, or what counts as one order, that affects every use case. Fixing this first saves you rework on everything that follows.
  • The data you need isn't being captured. No amount of clever technology creates data that doesn't exist. The first step then is a change to how you record things, and that takes time.
  • There's no owner for the source. If nobody is responsible for a dataset, it won't be maintained either, and your application will quietly degrade within six months.

Notice that none of these three is about technology or a missing platform. All three are about meaning and ownership. That's what the data foundation is really about. The rest is infrastructure, and infrastructure you can buy.

A half-day test

Want to know where you stand? Take one concrete decision you want AI to support, and try to reconstruct it by hand for ten past cases. If that takes an afternoon, your foundation is good enough. If it takes two weeks and you have to call three departments, you know exactly which part to fix first. And it's almost never the part the platform proposal was about.

title: AI governance without bureaucracy: what you need at minimum
excerpt: Governance nobody uses protects nobody. Four mechanisms that make the difference, and what you can safely skip.
metaTitle: AI Governance Without Bureaucracy: What You Actually Need
metaDescription: EU regulation requires organisations to demonstrably manage AI. Four light mechanisms beat a committee that slows everything down.
lede: EU regulation requires organisations to demonstrably manage AI. That can end up as a committee that slows everything down, or as four light mechanisms that make the work better.
summary: Classify your applications by risk, not by technology.
One register, one gate, one periodic check, one escalation path.
Heavy governance only where the risk justifies it.
summaryClose: Proportionality is the whole point of good governance.
takeaways: Register beats committee
Knowing what's running is ninety per cent of the control problem.
One gate, not a chain
If there are three approval points, people find a way around them.
Write down the "no" too
A documented rejection stops the same discussion coming back every quarter.
remember: Governance people work around is worse than no governance, because you think you're in control.
body:
The real risk of AI governance

The risk isn't that you regulate too little. The risk is that you regulate so much that people work around it, and you end up believing you're in control while a shadow practice grows with tools nobody knows about.

That happens faster than with classic IT, because AI tools are so easy to access. An employee who hits a six-week approval process can sort out the alternative themselves in two minutes with a credit card. Good governance accounts for that.

Start with risk classification, not technology

The mistake made most often: one regime for everything that's labelled "AI". That means a tool that writes up meeting notes has to go through the same process as a model that influences credit decisions. The result is predictable: the first gets slowed down for no reason, and the second doesn't get enough attention, because all the attention went to the avalanche of low-risk requests.

A workable three-level split:

  • Low: supports one employee, the output is reviewed directly by that person, no effect on anyone outside the organisation. Examples: summarising, draft text, searching internal documents. Regime: log it and apply general usage agreements.
  • Medium: influences a work process or a decision about a customer, with human review. Examples: preparing case files, prioritising requests, stock advice. Regime: logging, a named owner, a test set, periodic evaluation.
  • High: affects people's rights or interests, or operates without meaningful human review. Examples: credit scoring, candidate screening, fraud detection. Regime: full documentation, formal review beforehand, demonstrable oversight, logging.

The EU AI Act applies its own classification, with specific obligations per category and prohibited practices at the top end. It isn't limited to organisations established in the EU either: under Article 2 of the Act, it also reaches UK organisations that place an AI system on the EU market, or whose system's output is used in the EU. The UK has no AI Act of its own and regulates AI through existing sector regulators instead, applying shared principles rather than one cross-cutting law, as set out in the UK government's AI regulation: a pro-innovation approach. Have your legal department or a specialised adviser determine exactly where your applications fall under either framework. The split above is a working model to structure the internal conversation, not a legal judgement.

The four mechanisms you need at minimum

1. One register

A list of every AI application running or in development across the organisation, with for each one: owner, purpose, risk level, what data goes in, which supplier, and when it was last reviewed.

This sounds dull and it's the single most important thing you'll have. Without a register, you can't answer any other question. With one, you can find out who to talk to within an hour for any incident, audit question or supplier change.

Keep it light: a spreadsheet that's accurate beats a GRC module that's half filled in. What matters is that keeping it updated is a condition for going ahead, not a request made after the fact.

2. One gate

One moment where a new application is reviewed before it goes live. Not three, not a chain of departments waiting on each other. One meeting, with a fixed group (business, data/IT, risk) and a fixed turnaround time.

For low-risk applications, the gate is a ten-minute formality. For high-risk applications, it's a serious review. The difference is in the preparation, not the number of bodies involved.

Agree a maximum turnaround, say two weeks, and stick to it. The credibility of your governance depends more on this than on the content of your assessment framework.

3. One periodic check

AI applications degrade quietly. The world changes, the data shifts, the supplier updates the underlying model. Without a periodic check, you only notice once a user complains, and by then it's already been wrong for months.

A different rhythm per risk level: low risk, an annual check that it's still in use; medium risk, a six-monthly evaluation against the test set; high risk, quarterly with a documented outcome.

Important: the check should use a fixed test set made at the start. Without that set, you're testing a feeling, not a performance.

4. One escalation path

What does an employee do when they notice an AI application doing something odd? If the answer is "I don't know", nobody reports anything, and you only hear about it from a customer.

Make it concrete: one email address or form, a commitment to respond within two working days, and the authority to temporarily pause an application resting with one named person, without needing to convene a committee first. That last piece of authority makes the difference and is almost always forgotten.

What you can skip

Three things that often get built and rarely deliver anything:

  • A separate AI ethics committee alongside your existing risk structure. Usually better to add AI as a topic to the body that already exists: it already has a mandate and already meets.
  • A lengthy AI policy document before there are any applications. Policy written without practical experience is abstract and gets rewritten within a year. Start with five usage agreements on one page.
  • Tool choice as a governance question. Which platform you use is a procurement question. Which decisions you hand to it is the governance question.

Write down what you don't do, too

This is the part that gives the best return for the least work. If you decide not to build a particular application (AI-assisted staff appraisals, say), record why, who decided that, and when it will be looked at again.

Without that record, the same proposal comes back every quarter through a different route, and you have the same discussion each time with different people. With it, the conversation takes two minutes: here's the decision, here's the reasoning, and we'll look again in October.

title: Why AI pilots stall (and what to do about it)
excerpt: The pilot worked. Everyone was excited. And a year later, nothing has scaled up. Five causes, five countermeasures.
metaTitle: Why AI Pilots Stall (and What to Do About It)
metaDescription: Almost every organisation I speak to has successful AI pilots. Almost none have scaled up more than two. That's not a technology problem.
lede: Almost every organisation I speak to has successful AI pilots. Almost none have scaled up more than two. That's not a technology problem.
summary: A pilot proves feasibility, not value.
Scaling up fails on ownership, upkeep and work process, rarely on technology.
Agree the scale-up criteria before the pilot starts.
summaryClose: Whoever designs the pilot without exit criteria designs a dead end.
takeaways: Define success upfront
Without an agreed threshold set in advance, every outcome gets read as positive after the fact.
Upkeep belongs in the pilot
If nobody maintains it after delivery, scaling up is impossible by definition.
Pilot in the real environment
A pilot run outside the real work process only proves the technology works.
remember: A pilot with no agreed stop criterion never really ends, it just evaporates.
body:
The pilot paradox

Pilots are designed to reduce risk. Start small, learn, then scale up. In practice, they often do the opposite: they create the illusion of progress without anything actually changing. An organisation with seven successful pilots and zero applications in production is further from its goal than an organisation with one application that's actually running.

The causes are strikingly consistent. Five of them, and none are technical.

Cause 1: The pilot proved the wrong question

Most pilots answer the question "can this work technically?" These days, that answer is almost always yes, which means the pilot is neither informative nor decision-useful.

The questions that actually matter: does this cost less than it delivers at a hundred times this volume? Do the people who have to work with it actually want to use it when nobody's watching? Can we maintain it with the capacity we have?

Countermeasure: before you start, write down the one question the pilot needs to answer, and phrase it so that "no" is a possible answer. If you can't picture what a negative outcome looks like beforehand, you're not designing a pilot, you're putting on a demonstration.

Cause 2: The pilot ran outside the real work

To move fast, a pilot often gets set up alongside the existing process: a separate environment, a hand-picked group of enthusiastic users, a standalone dataset. That gets you a result quickly and tells you nothing about scalability.

What then goes wrong at scale-up: integration with the source system turns out to be three months of work, the average user doesn't have the context the pilot group had, and the real data is messier than the test dataset.

Countermeasure: a smaller scope in the real environment beats a larger scope alongside it. One team, real data, the real process, real integrations. That's slower in week one and considerably faster by month six.

Cause 3: Nobody owns the next phase

The pilot has a project lead. Their job is done at delivery. The business hasn't planned any capacity, reserved any budget, or set any target that this application fits into.

What happens then: the application keeps running in pilot form, unmaintained, until it breaks or the licence expires. Nobody decides anything. It just evaporates.

Countermeasure: name the scale-up owner before the pilot starts, not after. That person sits in the business, has budget, and sits on the pilot steering group. If you can't find that person, that's itself an important finding: apparently there's no place in the organisation where this value lands.

Cause 4: Upkeep wasn't factored in

AI applications need ongoing maintenance: quality monitoring, retraining or recalibration, tracking model versions, a test set that stays current. During the pilot phase, the project team does this implicitly. After delivery, nobody does.

This is why applications that worked fine in month one are quietly performing worse by month eight, without anyone noticing.

Countermeasure: include the upkeep cost in the business case, expressed in hours per month and assigned to a team. And during the pilot, run at least one real maintenance action (a retraining, a model update), so you know what it actually costs.

Cause 5: The organisation wasn't allowed to change

This is the deepest cause, and the one talked about least. An AI application that saves time means people do their work differently. Sometimes a role shifts. Sometimes a check moves from one department to another.

Pilots are often deliberately designed so these questions don't come up, because that makes things move faster. At scale-up, they all surface at once, and it turns out the business case only adds up if staffing or the division of work actually changes. That conversation was never prepared for.

Countermeasure: name at the start which organisational change is needed to realise the value, and check whether there's support for it. If the answer is that nothing is allowed to change, you can still run the pilot, but calculate the business case without the saving that change would require. Often a real, smaller value remains. That's a more honest starting point than a promise you can't keep later.

A one-page pilot contract

What works well in practice: before you start, write down five things on one page, signed by the sponsor and the scale-up owner.

  • The question this pilot answers, with a measurable threshold for "successful".
  • The stop criteria: at what outcome do we stop, and who decides that.
  • The scale-up owner: name, and the department where the value lands.
  • The upkeep estimate: how many hours a month does this cost after delivery, and who supplies them.
  • The change required: what has to be different in the work for the value to be realised.

This page takes an hour to write and prevents the scenario where, a year later, you have seven successful pilots and nothing in production. The biggest effect isn't in the document itself, but in the conversations you have to have to fill it in. That's exactly where the blockers become visible, while there's still time to fix them.
